id_and_class.theory_title: Nāgārjuna’s Empty Consciousness: Experience Without Essence
id_and_class.summary: Nāgārjuna argues that everything, consciousness included, is empty (śūnyatā) of svabhāva, an intrinsic nature that a thing would have from its own side. Experience is real conventionally and does causal work, but it arises only in dependence on faculty, object and conditions, with no intrinsic core and no ultimate subject to whom it belongs. The view refuses both illusionism and idealism, since both presuppose intrinsic nature: illusionism denies it to experience and idealism makes it foundational.

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Consciousness (vijñāna) is a dependently arisen, conventionally real event that lacks intrinsic nature. Nāgārjuna offers a diagnosis of what consciousness cannot be, not a positive theory of what it is.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: Neither mind nor matter has an intrinsic nature, so neither grounds the other. A conscious event arises from sense faculties, objects, bodily processes, attention, concepts and context, all of which are themselves empty.
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Not applicable (Nāgārjuna rejects intrinsic natures on both sides, so consciousness is neither a fundamental primitive nor a product of intrinsically physical bases; it is dependently arisen)
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: There is experience but no enduring experiencer behind it. A substantial self would have to be both cognitive subject and cognitive object, roles it cannot hold at once (MMK 9:3), so the subject position is occupied by different events at different moments.
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: Phenomenal qualities occur conventionally but have no irreducible qualitative core. Asking how intrinsic physical natures produce intrinsic phenomenal ones presupposes on both sides what Nāgārjuna denies.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: Only conventionally real, mutually dependent events: the five aggregates, six cognitive domains, causes and conditions. No dharmas with svabhāva, no substantial self, and no foundational consciousness.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: Awareness has no privileged reflexive access to itself. Instruments of knowledge and their objects establish each other, so no faculty can certify itself by inspecting its own features (Vigrahavyāvartanī).
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: Vijñāna is one of five aggregates making up a person and occurs across six domains: the five senses and mind. Its episodes depend both on occasioning conditions and on the conceptual processes that make them the episodes they are.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Phenomenal experience, perception, self-awareness, the self, causation, and liberation from suffering.
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Dependent origination is identical with emptiness: whatever arises dependently is empty, and nothing escapes dependent origination (MMK 24.18–19).
mechanism_and_dynamics.dynamics_of_emergence: Because consciousness lacks a fixed essence, it can arise, vary, interact and cease. An intrinsically fixed phenomenon could not enter relations that genuinely change it.
mechanism_and_dynamics.location_and_distribution: Consciousness is not located in a substance or witness. It occurs wherever its conditions come together, such as eye and visible form.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: Emptiness preserves causal efficacy. Nāgārjuna rejects arising from self, other, both or neither, and concludes that cause and effect are mutually dependent, not unreal.
mechanism_and_dynamics.integration_or_binding: The apparent unity of an agent is a systematic misapprehension; Nāgārjuna compares the agent to an illusion conjuring a further illusion (MMK 17:31–32).
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: Svabhāva is an automatic superimposition onto experience, a cognitive default that persists despite intellectual conviction, much as measuring the Müller-Lyer lines does not make them look equal.
core_claims_and_evidence: Consciousness arises in dependence on the eye and visible form (MMK 3:7), and an eye that saw by its own nature would have to see independently of anything seen.
Vision cannot see itself, so awareness is not self-establishing; later Madhyamaka authors rejected reflexive awareness (svasaṃvedana) on this basis.
There is no substantial self and no substantial basis, such as the aggregates, from which a merely imputed self could be built.
Emptiness is itself empty: a corrective to a misconception, not a newly discovered ultimate nature.
mechanism_and_dynamics.basis_of_belief_or_evidence_type: Philosophical and soteriological: case-by-case dialectical refutation of intrinsic natures, aimed at pacifying conceptual proliferation (prapañca).

empirics_and_critiques.criticisms_and_tensions: Critics such as Burton press the nihilism charge: if nothing ultimately exists, conventional truth has nothing to be about. Nāgārjuna's claim to have no thesis (Vigrahavyāvartanī 29) seems to assert exactly what it forbids, and global mind-dependence is hard to state for things like mountains when the minds themselves are empty.
empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: Whether the position can be stated without self-refutation, and whether it leads to genuine paradox at the limits of thought (Priest and Garfield). Whether its handling of the hard problem is a dissolution or an evasion depends on the assessor's own ontology.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: Consistent as an ontology without foundations, a structure Priest and Garfield have taken up in contemporary work on grounding and metaphysical dependence. Its placement under Idealism is uneasy, since it explicitly denies consciousness foundational status.

survival_beyond_death.rationale: No substantial self exists to survive, yet conventional agency and moral consequence are preserved; the view denies an enduring experiencer without answering what continues.

meaning_and_purpose.rationale: The analysis serves liberation: only a being without fixed essence can be freed from suffering, and nirvāṇa is the end of misapprehending this world, not a move to another.
